title: The Ground Under Buenos Aires: exile, the trowel, and a discipline invented in order to have a subject
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The City Before Anyone Digs It

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first of November
stops.date_confidence: attested; es.wikipedia gives the full date of birth
stops.campa: On the first of November, 1950, a son is born to the Schávelzon family in Buenos Aires. The city he enters reads itself entirely from paper: chronicles, land grants, the memoirs of its own founders. Nobody asks what lies under the asphalt, because nobody yet holds that the ground of a modern capital is a document at all. The cisterns, cellars, rubbish pits and colonial footings beneath his birthplace will wait thirty-four years for him to come back and open them. He is named Daniel Gastón, and he grows up standing on the archive he will spend his life excavating.
suggested_refs: Street-level photographs of central Buenos Aires around 1950, the surface of the city before any urban excavation

stops.name: Facultad de Arquitectura, the training in structures
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the degree is attested but the source gives no years, and the campus buildings of his student period are unconfirmed. Date defaulted to the decade
stops.campa: He studies architecture at the Universidad de Buenos Aires, in a country where urban archaeology does not exist as a discipline and where nobody is training anyone to look for it. Architecture teaches him to read a building before anyone tells him what it means: load and span, the seam where one century's masonry meets another's, the patch that betrays a wall rebuilt. It is a training in evidence that happens to be made of brick and lime, and he keeps it long after he stops designing buildings, turning the same eye downward.
suggested_refs: The FADU pavilion at Ciudad Universitaria, later home of the Instituto de Arte Americano and the Centro de Arqueología Urbana

segments.name: Exile on the Coast, Exile in the Valley

stops.name: Manabí coast, the Manteña excavations
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact and the year of exile; the specific Manteña site is named in no accessed source, so the point approximates the Manabí coastal region
stops.campa: The military take the country in 1976 and he leaves it, crossing to the Ecuadorian coast rather than to Europe. On the shore of Manabí he excavates a site of the Manteña culture, the seafaring people whose rafts worked this coast before any Spaniard charted it. Exile does not interrupt the work; it moves it. Under a different sky he digs the question he will later dig at home, which is what the ground keeps when the written record either lies or was never made, and who is permitted to read the answer.
suggested_refs: Manteña ceramic and stone material from the Manabí coast, the subject of his first excavations in exile

stops.name: Ciudad Universitaria, Mexico: the doctorate
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the degrees are attested at UNAM but the source gives no graduation year. A date range of 1978-1983 circulates without attribution and is not adopted here
stops.campa: At the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México he takes a master's degree and then a doctorate in architecture, entering the first generation of Latin Americans to hold such a doctorate and, by his own country's reckoning, the first Argentine among them. Mexico gives him the prehispanic restoration trade: pyramids opened by tunnel, plaster read like a page, a mound understood as an accumulation of separate decisions across a thousand years. No building there is a single moment, and someone has to unpick the sequence course by course.
suggested_refs: The doctoral theses of the first generation of Latin American architecture PhDs at UNAM

stops.name: Lima, the UNESCO subsidy
stops.date_confidence: attested; the es.wikipedia Premios section reads 'Subsidio de la UNESCO (PNUD, Lima), 1981'. Physical travel to Lima is not claimed
stops.campa: UNESCO, through the development programme office at Lima, awards him a subsidy in 1981 for his research. He is thirty, stateless in practice, and the money arrives from a regional body rather than from any national science council, the council of his own country being in the hands of the men who drove him out. The subsidy pays for work on coastlines and pyramids belonging to no government that would claim him, and it is entered afterwards at the head of his list of awards, the earliest one there.
suggested_refs: The UNDP regional office at Lima, channel for UNESCO research subsidies in the early 1980s

stops.name: Mexico City, the long tie to the INAH
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the consulting and visiting role is attested but undated, and the point is a proxy for the INAH headquarters rather than a confirmed address
stops.campa: He keeps a footing at the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia long after the student years close, returning as visiting scholar and consultant across decades. The dictatorship that sent him north will fall; the institution that received the exile does not release him. Mexico remains the second country of his working life, the place where the vocabulary of stratigraphy and restoration entered his hands, and where a young Argentine with no country to dig in was handed other people's ruins to practise on.
suggested_refs: INAH restoration files from the prehispanic projects of the late 1970s and early 1980s

segments.name: The Return, and a Discipline Founded

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo, the return under Alfonsín
stops.date_confidence: attested for the month and the invitation; the square is the symbolic seat of the government that called him back, not a confirmed point of arrival
stops.campa: In February 1984, with the elected government two months old, he comes back at the invitation of President Alfonsín. He returns to found what did not exist: a Programa de Arqueología Urbana at the university, and with it the claim that the capital's own ground deserves the care given to a Mexican pyramid. Buenos Aires has always told its history from documents written by the literate. He proposes to interrogate the part nobody wrote down, beginning under the square where the country announces itself.
suggested_refs: The founding papers of the Programa de Arqueología Urbana, Universidad de Buenos Aires, 1984

stops.name: CONICET, the appointment that makes it a career
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted. Point corrected to the Polo Científico Tecnológico at Godoy Cruz 2290, the council's seat
stops.campa: He enters CONICET as a researcher in 1985, and the discipline he is inventing acquires an institutional spine. It stops being one man with a trowel and a university permit; it becomes a line item, a career track, a place from which students can be paid to learn stratigraphy in a city that has never trained an urban archaeologist. He will hold the post for more than three decades, and the centre he founds six years later is built on this salary line.
suggested_refs: CONICET researcher files for the first urban archaeology positions in Argentina

stops.name: Caserón de Rosas, footings under the park
stops.date_confidence: attested for the winter of 1985 by the CAU chronology; month approximated within that season
stops.campa: In the winter of 1985 he opens the lawns of the Parque Tres de Febrero, where Juan Manuel de Rosas kept the Caserón, the great house from which he governed the Confederation and which his enemies demolished after Caseros so thoroughly that a park was laid over the hole. Footings surface under grass that generations of porteños have crossed without knowing. The Restorer of the Laws survives here as brick courses and broken plates, and what the trenches recover is mostly the shape of the demolition his enemies ordered.
suggested_refs: Nineteenth-century views of the Caserón de Rosas at Palermo, demolished after 1852

stops.name: Mendoza, the Cabildo on the founding ground
stops.date_confidence: attested for the start of the Mendoza work in 1985; month and day defaulted. Point corrected to the Área Fundacional at Plaza Pedro del Castillo, site of the colonial Cabildo
stops.campa: From 1985 the method travels west to Mendoza, where he excavates the colonial Cabildo on the founding ground by the Plaza Pedro del Castillo. The city that stood here was levelled by the earthquake of 1861 and rebuilt on new land to the southwest, leaving its whole first self underground and undisturbed. Every layer he opens is a layer of catastrophe. Mendoza offers what Buenos Aires never will, a colonial town that was not built over but simply abandoned where it fell.
suggested_refs: The Museo del Área Fundacional at Mendoza, built over the excavated colonial Cabildo

stops.name: Manzana de las Luces, the tunnel article
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the article is cited with journal, number, month and page range
stops.campa: In May 1988 the magazine Todo es Historia carries twenty-seven pages by him under the title Los túneles de Buenos Aires: 140 años entre la memoria y el olvido. The city has believed for a century and a half in a secret network under its colonial blocks, dug for smuggling, for escape, for Jesuit conspiracy. He does not deny that tunnels exist beneath the Manzana de las Luces. He insists on surveying them block by block and vault by vault, and on reporting what each one was actually dug for.
suggested_refs: Todo es Historia no. 251, May 1988, pp. 8-35; the surviving colonial passages under the Manzana de las Luces
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Manzana de las Luces', citing Todo es Historia no. 251 (May 1988), pp. 8-35

stops.name: Instituto de Arte Americano, the centre founded
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the es.wikipedia article on the Centro de Arqueología Urbana
stops.campa: On the seventh of May, 1991, inside the Instituto de Arte Americano at the architecture faculty, he founds the Centro de Arqueología Urbana. It is the first such centre in the country: a permanent address for a practice he has carried for seven years from one rescue dig to the next. Builders find something, a ministry telephones, a team goes. From now on there is a place where the telephone rings, a store for the finds, and students who came to study architecture and leave knowing how to read a floor.
stops.quote: Could it be true that beneath the floor lies the past? Yes, without any doubt; every day we walk, work, and eat on top of what has already happened.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'El futuro del pasado: Indagaciones en arqueología urbana,' in Ciudad y ciudadanos (Buenos Aires: Paidós, 2002), p. 199; translation by the researcher
suggested_refs: The founding act of the Centro de Arqueología Urbana, 7 May 1991, Instituto de Arte Americano, FADU-UBA

stops.name: Cabildo de Buenos Aires, under the town hall
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1991-1992 by the excavation list in the Schávelzon article alone; the Cabildo and CAU articles do not corroborate it. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He digs beneath the Cabildo on the Plaza de Mayo, the colonial town hall where the men of 1810 argued a viceroy out of office. The building above ground has been cut back twice by street widening and rebuilt to suit each century's idea of what a founding monument should look like. Below it the strata answer with something less ceremonious: the drains, floors and refuse of a small mud port at the edge of an empire, laid down long before anyone here had a nation to be proud of.
suggested_refs: Arqueología e historia del Cabildo de Buenos Aires (1995), his report on the excavation

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the founding book of the field
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The same year Corregidor publishes Arqueología histórica de Buenos Aires, and a field acquires its founding book. Until now the city's archaeology has lived in permits, site reports and conference papers; here it is set out as a discipline with a method, a chronology of local and imported ceramics, and an argument that a colonial capital is as legitimate an object as any prehispanic site. Students who will spend careers under the pavements of Argentina learn the trade from it. He is forty, and the subject is now teachable.
suggested_refs: Arqueología histórica de Buenos Aires (Corregidor, 1991), first edition

stops.name: Imprenta Coni, the floor of the trade
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the excavation and publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In 1994 he excavates the site of the Imprenta Coni in San Telmo, one of the oldest printing houses of Buenos Aires, whose presses turned out the official gazettes, the medical journals and the schoolbooks of a republic teaching itself to read. He recovers no manuscripts. He recovers the floor of the trade: type fragments, ink residue, the discarded metal of a working shop, a history usually told through the words that came off the presses and read here from the presses instead.
stops.quote: Material culture is the 'social life of things,' as it has become fashionable to say in recent years: objects in their relations with society, production, consumption, circulation, and discard.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'El futuro del pasado' (Paidós, 2002), p. 201; translation by the researcher
suggested_refs: Type fragments and printing debris recovered from the Imprenta Coni site, San Telmo
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Daniel Schávelzon', bibliography and excavation lists

stops.name: Michelangelo, cellars under a tango house
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the site is attested in his excavation list but undated in any accessed source. Date placed within the centre's first decade
stops.campa: Under the Michelangelo on Balcarce, a tango house for tourists in a converted colonial building, he opens cellars and a cistern belonging to the eighteenth-century merchant town. The room above sells the neighbourhood's story nightly in the form of a floor show; the room below holds the version nobody staged. Both rooms are ways the neighbourhood keeps telling itself what it was, and only one of the two can be checked against the objects people actually threw away.
stops.quote: Excavating a 19th-century garbage pit in Buenos Aires means coming face to face with a universe of objects of foreign origin, in a proportion of up to 90%.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'Argentina and Great Britain: Studying an Asymmetrical Relationship through Domestic Material Culture,' Historical Archaeology 47(1) (2013), p. 11
suggested_refs: The colonial cellars and cistern beneath the former Michelangelo, calle Balcarce, San Telmo

stops.name: Altos de Ezcurra, the household under the floor
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the site appears in his excavation list, tagged as a single-source claim, and is undated in any accessed source
stops.campa: On Defensa he works the Altos de Ezcurra, a colonial house of the family of Encarnación Ezcurra, who ran her husband's street politics in the eighteen-thirties with a harder hand than he did. Restored and reopened as a cultural site, its rooms present the polite version. Beneath the floors lies the plainer sequence: a merchant household's dishes, bottles and sweepings, imported crockery and local coarseware together in one fill, the daily part of the story that no portrait of the family records.
stops.quote: There were enormous differences between British objects to be used at a reception in a high-status home and a small African religious symbol etched on the base of an old plate, or a slave's small pipe; but they all played a social role.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'Argentina and Great Britain,' Historical Archaeology 47(1) (2013), p. 19
suggested_refs: The Altos de Ezcurra on calle Defensa, colonial house of the Ezcurra family

stops.name: Museo Etnográfico, a museum of museums
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the excavation is attested but undated, and the 1905-1927 building phases rest on the biography alone
stops.campa: Under the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti he finds the museum itself: the building phases of its own first decades, roughly 1905 to 1927, walls and floors that later renovations paved over without recording. An institution built to hold other people's material culture turns out to be a stratified site like any other, its extensions and demolitions legible only by digging. The building that keeps the past for a living kept almost no record of itself.
stops.quote: Porque lo que importa para la arqueología no es la riqueza o el lujo o la calidad estética de los objetos, ya que éstos no son más que una parte de las respuestas a preguntas que nos hacemos sobre el pasado. Por más simples y modestos, por más feos y socialmente despreciables que sean, nos indican acerca de quienes los usaron.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'El futuro del pasado' (Paidós, 2002), p. 201, original Spanish
suggested_refs: Building plans of the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti, 1905-1927 phases

stops.name: Parque Lezama, the disputed first city
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the work at Parque Lezama and the Museo Histórico Nacional is attested but undated in accessed sources
stops.campa: He works the slope of Parque Lezama, where the Museo Histórico Nacional stands and where tradition places the first founding of Buenos Aires by Pedro de Mendoza in 1536. His centre publishes on that first city, the settlement of 1536 to 1541 that starved and burned and was given up, under a title that sets history against myth. The documents cannot fix the site and the ground has yet to produce it. He digs the slope the legend names, on the grounds that the legend is what sends anyone here to look in the first place.
suggested_refs: Centro de Arqueología Urbana, 'Arqueología de la primera Buenos Aires (1536-1541): entre la historia y el mito'
sources: Centro de Arqueología Urbana publications, cited in pedro_de_mendoza.journey.json

stops.name: New York, the Guggenheim fellowship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the category on the Foundation's own fellows listing; month and day defaulted. Physical travel to New York is inferred, not confirmed
stops.campa: In 1994 the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation names him a fellow in the history and theory of architecture, ten years after his return and a decade of trenches. The award reaches a man who has been arguing, one rescue dig at a time, that a colonial port's rubbish deserves the attention normally reserved for pyramids and cathedrals. His subject, increasingly, is the traffic between Buenos Aires and Britain: whose plates, whose bottles, whose terms of trade, and who was doing the buying.
stops.quote: to use a particularly Argentinean idiom ... it takes two to tango.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'Argentina and Great Britain,' Historical Archaeology 47(1) (2013), p. 22
suggested_refs: The 1994 Guggenheim fellows listing, Architecture, Planning and Design: History, Theory and Criticism
sources: John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation, official fellows page (gf.org)

stops.name: National Gallery of Art, the senior fellowship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by es.wikipedia; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The same year he holds a senior fellowship at the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts, in the National Gallery of Art at Washington, among specialists in painting, sculpture and connoisseurship. He brings them a demolished customs house, a buried convent floor, a crate of transfer-printed sherds out of a latrine. The claim he makes in that company is the one he makes everywhere: that these are visual documents of the first order, illegible only because nobody has gone down after them.
suggested_refs: CASVA annual reports for 1994, listing the year's senior fellows

stops.name: Dumbarton Oaks, three returns
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1996, 2006 and 2008 in the es.wikipedia Premios list, quoted verbatim; the institution's own fellows pages returned a 404 and could not confirm. Point corrected to 1703 32nd Street NW
stops.campa: Three times across a dozen years the Washington research library of Dumbarton Oaks supports him, with a grant, a fellowship and an award, in 1996, 2006 and 2008. Built for the study of Byzantium and pre-Columbian America, its reading rooms and formal gardens in Georgetown make a strange counterpart to a cistern in San Telmo. Each stay pays for another season of fieldwork at home. The Latin American archaeology the institution collects is, in his case, being made at the same time it is being read.
suggested_refs: Dumbarton Oaks pre-Columbian studies programme records, 1996 to 2008

stops.name: UNESCO, Place de Fontenoy: the heritage lists
stops.date_confidence: the consultancy is attested and quoted directly; it is undated, and travel to the Paris headquarters is not evidenced. Date placed mid-career as a marker
stops.campa: He serves as a consultant to UNESCO on World Heritage declarations, applying to a continent the judgement he applies to a single block of Monserrat: what is irreplaceable, what is merely old, and what a state will actually defend once the plaque is fixed to the wall. The work sits oddly beside his own trade. Most of what he excavates is condemned in advance, dug precisely because a builder is coming, and the list of what the world agrees to save has never had much room for a rubbish pit.
suggested_refs: Latin American World Heritage nomination dossiers of the period, on which he consulted

stops.name: Ruinas de San Francisco, the ruin that refused
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1998 publication and for a directorship of roughly two decades; month and day defaulted. Point corrected to the Área Fundacional, Ituzaingó y Beltrán, and is best available rather than verified
stops.campa: For roughly twenty years he directs the research centre at the Ruinas de San Francisco in Mendoza, the shell of a church begun by the Jesuits, handed to the Franciscans after the expulsion of 1767, and left broken by the earthquake of 1861. The province never rebuilt it. The ruin stands as a memorial nobody restored, and the decision to leave the collapse where it fell is part of what he records, against the ordinary instinct to tidy a disaster away before anyone has read it.
suggested_refs: Las ruinas de San Francisco, arqueología e historia (1998)

stops.name: Barrancas de San Isidro, the slope on its side
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2001 publication; the excavation itself is undated in accessed sources. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: With Mario Silveira he digs the barrancas of San Isidro, the wooded bluffs north of the capital where colonial quintas looked out over a river that has since pulled back behind its own silt. He publishes the excavations in 2001. Each terrace on the slope belongs to a different century of the same view, cut by people who assumed the water would stay where it was. The quintas above the bluff sold themselves on the river, and the river left, putting a mile of reclaimed ground between the terraces and the water they were sited for.
suggested_refs: Excavaciones arqueológicas en San Isidro (2001)

stops.name: Alta Gracia, the house of the viceroy Liniers
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the site appears in his study list but is undated in accessed sources
stops.campa: In Alta Gracia he studies the house of Santiago de Liniers, the French officer who retook Buenos Aires from the British in 1806, was made viceroy for it, and was shot by firing squad six years later for refusing the revolution. The house outlives every reversal of his fortune and stands now as a museum in the estancia the Jesuits built. He reads its walls, floors and service yards for the working household that the man's own biography never bothered to record.
suggested_refs: The Casa del Virrey Liniers at Alta Gracia, in the former Jesuit estancia

stops.name: Paraná, the Barrio del Tambor
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the work is attested but undated in accessed sources
stops.campa: At Paraná he maps the Barrio del Tambor and the ground around the Capilla San Miguel Arcángel, the quarter of an Afro-Argentine community that official history preferred not to record and afterwards reported as having vanished. The chapel still stands. The neighbourhood survives chiefly in what lies under it. A national story insisting the black population simply disappeared meets, in Entre Ríos, the ordinary domestic evidence of people who lived here and were counted out of the account.
suggested_refs: The Capilla San Miguel Arcángel and the traced footprint of the Barrio del Tambor, Paraná

stops.name: Puerto Deseado, the founding ground
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the site appears in his work list but is undated in accessed sources
stops.campa: On the Patagonian coast he works the Área Fundacional of Puerto Deseado, the founding ground of a settlement on a bay charted by Thomas Cavendish and later surveyed from the Beagle. It lies a thousand miles from the colonial capital, in a province that had almost no colony to speak of, and the method does not change with the latitude. The far south is full of towns whose founding is remembered chiefly by a monument raised long afterwards, and he goes to the ground under the monument.
suggested_refs: The Área Fundacional of Puerto Deseado on the Ría Deseado, Santa Cruz

stops.name: Ushuaia, the town the prison built
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the work on Ushuaia's archaeology, history and heritage is attested but undated in accessed sources
stops.campa: At the southern edge of the continent he documents the archaeology, history and heritage of Ushuaia, a town whose streets and public buildings were largely raised by the convicts of its own penal colony. As far from the cobbles of San Telmo as the country reaches, he arrives with the identical question: what does this ground hold that the records left out, and who benefited from the leaving out. The prison built the town, and the town spent most of a century preferring not to say so.
suggested_refs: The penal colony buildings of Ushuaia, raised by prisoner labour

stops.name: Roque Pérez, the house of Perón
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2009 publication; month and day defaulted. Point corrected to 35 degrees 25 minutes S, 59 degrees 19 minutes W. The birthplace dispute between Lobos and Roque Pérez is left open
stops.campa: In the town of Roque Pérez he studies a modest rural house associated with the childhood of Juan Domingo Perón, and publishes La casa de Perón in 2009. Whether the boy was born at Lobos, as the official record has it, or here, as a revisionist tradition insists, is exactly the sort of question the documents have argued to a standstill. He brings a trowel to a fight about a birth certificate. The building is treated as what it is: a small provincial house with a long history of alterations.
suggested_refs: La casa de Perón (2009); the disputed birth house at Roque Pérez
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Daniel Schávelzon', bibliography and site list

stops.name: Plaza Roberto Arlt, the quiet dead
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by the CAU chronology; day defaulted
stops.campa: In March 2000 his team examines bone remains turned up at Plaza Roberto Arlt, an unglamorous square in the downtown grid that proves to hold its own quiet dead. The plaza carries the name of the man who wrote the city's furious underside, its cheats and boarding houses and small desperate schemes. Under his name the work is literal: the actual remains of people the city processed and set down without ceremony, surfacing between office blocks in the middle of a working week.
stops.quote: Urban archaeology allows us to penetrate, if only a little, into the life, the sufferings and the joys of those people, trying to understand how they lived, worked, or understood the world around them.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'El futuro del pasado' (Paidós, 2002), p. 204; translation by the researcher
suggested_refs: The CAU field report on the human remains recovered at Plaza Roberto Arlt, March 2000

stops.name: The colonial core, a convent of 1745
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by the CAU chronology; the specific convent is not named in any accessed source, so the point is provisional within the historic core
stops.campa: In August 2001 a restoration project brings the team back to a convent structure of 1745 in the colonial core. Every such call is the same negotiation conducted against a schedule: the owners want a building fit for modern use, the contractor wants the floor closed by Friday, and the archaeologist insists the fabric be read before it is covered for another century. Fifteen years into the work, he has never once had a site that was not being handed back to a builder on a date already fixed.
suggested_refs: CAU chronology entry for the August 2001 convent restoration project

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the black book of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Emecé publishes Buenos Aires Negra in 2003, and he turns the method on the city's own dark repertoire: its crimes, its hauntings, its stories of what happened in this cellar and that convent. He does not set out to spoil the tales. He sets out to ask which of them left anything behind, since a rumour and a massacre differ chiefly in that one of the two is still in the ground. The book sells to readers who came for ghosts and are handed stratigraphy instead.
stops.quote: There was thus defined a city where the inhabitants were mostly foreign, where no ties were formed with the past, nor a collective memory established, all managed by a social class in power that took no concern in economic interests for national development, only in its own.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'Argentina and Great Britain,' Historical Archaeology 47(1) (2013), p. 21
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires Negra (Emecé, 2003)

stops.name: Manzana de las Luces, the tunnels in a book
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Seventeen years after the magazine article he returns to the tunnels in a book of their own. By now his teams have been down enough of them to say what they are: cisterns, drains, cellars connecting one property to the next, the water and waste engineering of a town without pipes, and under the Manzana de las Luces a genuine colonial passage that is not a smugglers' road to the river. The legend survives the correction easily. He publishes the correction anyway, with plans and sections.
suggested_refs: Túneles de Buenos Aires (2005); surveyed plans of the passages beneath the Manzana de las Luces

stops.name: Plaza Colón, the customs house underground
stops.date_confidence: the site belongs to his register of Buenos Aires archaeology; the systematic excavation of 2009 to 2011 was directed by Sandra Guillermo under the Instituto Nacional de Antropología, not by him. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Behind the government house at Plaza Colón lie the curved brick foundations of the Aduana Taylor, the customs house Edward Taylor built in 1855 and the city pulled down in 1894, the gate through which the imported nineteenth century arrived by the crate. The site belongs to the register of Buenos Aires archaeology he has spent a career assembling; the systematic excavation there, from 2009 to 2011, is directed by Sandra Guillermo. The river that fed the building now lies half a kilometre off behind landfill.
stops.quote: Buenos Aires has long called itself the Paris of South America.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'Argentina and Great Britain,' Historical Archaeology 47(1) (2013), p. 11
suggested_refs: The glazed roof over the excavated Aduana Taylor foundations, Museo Casa Rosada, since 2011
sources: Instituto Nacional de Antropología, Aduana Taylor excavation record

stops.name: San Ignacio, seventeenth century in a service trench
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by the CAU chronology; day defaulted
stops.campa: In September 2012 work under the pavements near the church of San Ignacio brings up seventeenth-century material, the earliest colonial fabric of the city, lying no deeper than a service trench for pipes and cable. Above it people cross to the corner without looking down. Four hundred years compress into a cut a metre across, and the sequence runs unbroken from the mud-walled port to the sandwich wrappers. Each generation of the city built on the discards of the last.
stops.quote: Garbage, the forgotten, the lost, the hidden, the foundations of a collapsed house, or the marbles children lost in the street when they still played with them: layer upon layer, they build up an immense fill on which we live as if it were an enormous onion.
stops.quote_source: Daniel Schávelzon, 'El futuro del pasado' (Paidós, 2002), p. 200; translation by the researcher

segments.name: Teyú Cuaré, and the Archive of an Excavator

stops.name: Teyú Cuaré, the walls in the forest
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year in the Schávelzon article alone; the park's own encyclopedia article makes no mention of the ruins or the study, and period press coverage was never fetched. Point corrected to the park. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In 2015, working with Ana Igareta, he excavates stone structures hidden in the forest above the Paraná at Teyú Cuaré, in Misiones, and reports them as a refuge built in anticipation of a German defeat in the war, prepared for men who in the end never needed to hide so far from a road. The story has circulated for decades as rumour. The excavation gives it walls, coins and dates, and the international press takes hold of the find and makes of it something considerably larger than the report says.
suggested_refs: The stone structures of Teyú Cuaré provincial park, San Ignacio, Misiones

stops.name: Ciudad Universitaria, the tribute volume
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the full title; the title's count of thirty years does not agree with the centre's founding on 7 May 1991, which makes 2016 its twenty-fifth. The discrepancy is left standing
stops.campa: In 2016 Archaeopress of Oxford publishes Easter Island Archaeology: A Tribute to Daniel Schavelzon on the 30th Anniversary of the Center for Urban Archaeology at the University of Buenos Aires, edited by Mario Silveira. The colleagues who assemble it are the people the centre trained. The count of years belongs to whoever is counting; the centre itself dates from May 1991, and the programme before it from the first summer of the restored democracy. A field that had no practitioners when he began has enough of them to fill a volume.
suggested_refs: Easter Island Archaeology: A Tribute to Daniel Schavelzon, ed. M. Silveira (Archaeopress, Oxford, 2016)

stops.name: Albuquerque, the papers go north
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the donation; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: From 2017 his personal papers go to the Latin American Collection at the University of New Mexico: correspondence, manuscripts, field photographs, and family documents that include images of Russia and Poland from the eighteen-nineties, the only trace anywhere of where the family came from before Buenos Aires. An excavator's archive becomes a deposit in its own right, ordered by somebody else's system, to be worked through one day by a reader who never met him.
suggested_refs: The Schávelzon papers in the Latin American Collection, University of New Mexico

stops.name: Biblioteca Nacional, the library comes to rest
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the donation; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Portions of his personal library go the other way, to the Biblioteca Nacional in Buenos Aires. Forty years of reading on colonial ceramics, urban history, restoration and the material culture of the River Plate come to rest in the city whose ground taught him the subject. Books that were working tools become holdings, catalogued and shelved above the barrancas of Recoleta, in a building raised on the site of the presidential residence that was pulled down in 1958.
suggested_refs: The Biblioteca Nacional at Agüero 2502, on the site of the demolished presidential residence

stops.name: CONICET, the end of the appointment
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of retirement; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In 2018 he retires from CONICET after more than three decades on its rolls. The council he joined in 1985 to fund a discipline that did not exist now supports urban archaeologists in half the provinces of the country, working under plazas, churches, estancias and highways. He does not stop publishing. What ends is the salary and the formal affiliation, and by now the field he entered alone has enough hands in it to carry on without his name on the permits.
suggested_refs: CONICET service record, 1985 to 2018

stops.name: Casa Rosada, rescue on the fort's ground
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In 2019 he publishes on rescue archaeology at the Casa Rosada, the ground where the Spanish fort of Buenos Aires stood until 1873 and where the government of the republic has sat ever since. It is the most photographed patch of soil in the country, and, until the builders open it, among the least examined. The work is rescue, which means it happens because something else is being built, on a schedule set by engineers, in the narrow window between the discovery and the pour.
suggested_refs: Arqueología de rescate en Casa Rosada (2019)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a war excavated at a distance
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: With Ana Igareta he publishes Arqueología de la Segunda Guerra Mundial en Sudamérica in 2022, extending to a continent the work begun in the Misiones forest: the refuges, the internment sites, the sunken hulls, the material residue of a European war fought at a distance by countries that mostly declared themselves neutral. He is seventy-one. The shelf behind him runs past eighty books, and the discipline he had to invent in order to have a subject is now taught in universities he never worked at.
suggested_refs: Arqueología de la Segunda Guerra Mundial en Sudamérica, with Ana Igareta (2022)
